nameStory: This little crustacean gets its name from its impressive jumping ability and sandy beach habitat - when disturbed, it can hop several times its body length! The 'sand flea' nickname comes from both its bouncing behavior and its tiny size, though it's not actually a flea at all but rather a relative of shrimp and lobsters.
description: The Platensis sand flea is a small, laterally compressed crustacean that looks like a tiny shrimp curved on its side. These beach-dwelling amphipods are typically brownish or grayish in color, helping them blend in with the sand and seaweed where they live. They're quite small, usually less than an inch long, with a segmented body and long antennae. Despite their tiny size, they're incredibly active jumpers that seem to appear out of nowhere when you disturb beach wrack.

idTips.label: Jumping behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, these creatures explode into action with powerful spring-like jumps that can launch them several inches - much farther than you'd expect for something so small

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened from side to side like a tiny curved shrimp, with a hunched back that gives them their characteristic comma-like profile

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Mottled brown to gray coloration that feels slightly rough to the touch, perfectly matching the dried seaweed and sand where they hide

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of thread-like antennae that are constantly twitching and feeling around - often the first thing you notice moving in beach debris

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found burrowed in or under piles of dried seaweed and organic debris along the high tide line, where it feels damp and slightly cool

habitat: Look for these sand fleas along New England's sandy beaches in the wrack zone - that line of dried seaweed, driftwood, and organic debris left by high tides. They prefer areas where the sand stays slightly moist underneath the surface layer, typically 10-50 feet back from the water's edge. You'll find them from Maine's rocky coasts to Cape Cod's expansive beaches, wherever organic matter accumulates above the normal wave reach.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm, often found in large numbers under fresh piles of seaweed washed up by spring storms. This is when they're easiest to spot as they haven't yet burrowed deeply.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when populations are highest. Look for them during cooler morning or evening hours, as they tend to burrow deeper into cooler sand during hot midday sun.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active through autumn, especially after storms bring fresh organic material to shore. Their jumping seems more sluggish as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, as they burrow deeper into sand for insulation. Only the hardiest individuals remain near the surface during winter beach walks.

funFact: These tiny beach acrobats can jump using a spring-loaded tail mechanism - they curl their abdomen under their body like a loaded catapult, then snap it straight to launch themselves through the air with enough force to escape from predators many times their size!
confusionNotes: Often confused with actual fleas or small insects, but remember that sand fleas are crustaceans with segmented bodies and long antennae, while true fleas are insects with six legs and no visible antennae. Sand fleas also can't bite you - they're harmless detritus feeders, not blood-suckers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sand fleas,' these creatures are completely unrelated to the biting fleas that bother pets - they're actually more closely related to the shrimp on your dinner plate! The name confusion has led many beachgoers to unnecessarily fear these harmless and beneficial beach cleaners.
compareHints: Since this is the only Platorchestia species commonly found in New England, compare it to other beach amphipods in the sandhopper family by its relatively large size and powerful jumping ability. Other beach amphipods tend to be smaller and more likely to scurry rather than leap when disturbed, and most lack the distinctive hunched-back profile of Platorchestia platensis.
